newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: World's top fighter jets vie for S.Korean contracts.
newsitem.headline: World's top fighter jets vie for S.Korean contracts.

text.p: Fighter jets from Russia, France and the United States roared across the Seoul sky at the weekend as the three countries enter the final stage of a dogfight for one of the world's most lucrative air defence contracts.

The inaugural Seoul Air Show, a stage for South Korea's burgeoning aerospace industry, will open its doors on Monday in an atmopshere of fierce competition to grab contracts worth billions of dollars to modernise the South Korean air force.

Over 200 aerospace and defence industry exhibitors from 21 nations will display goods at the seven-day trade show, eyeing Seoul's plans to spend 20 trillion won ($24 billion) by 2010 on fighter jets, surveillance planes and other defence equipment.

On Saturday, as French, U.S. and Russian warplanes put on impressive displays, international air defence contractors began a scramble for a slice of South Korea's rapidly growing aerospace industry and air defence projects.

The top three contenders for South Korea's fighter jet programme are France's Dassault Aviation's Rafale fighter jet, the U.S. Air Force's F/A-18 Hornet developed by McDonnell Douglas Corp and Russia's Sukhoi Su-30.
"Those are the three main candidates," said a European exhibitor as manufacturers began setting up booths in the main conference hall.
"While the French are offering a lot of technical know-how, it would be very difficult for South Korea to turn its back on its long relationship with the U.S," he said.
The United States maintains 37,000 troops in South Korea.

The sight of Russian fighter jets thundering across the skyline of Seoul Airport to win favour with South Koera's defence ministry marks a new era on the Korean peninsula, the world's last remaining Cold War frontier.

South Korea technically remains at war with communist North Korea, whose military has traditionally been backed by Moscow. A fragile ceasefire has kept the peace on the Korean peninsula since the end of the 1950-53 Korean War.
With industry talk of a possible imminent takeover by South Korea's Samsung Aerospace Industries Co Ltd of bankrupt Dutch planemaker Fokker, South Korea's skyward ambitions are being taken seriously.
But despite heavy speculation by industry analysts and local press, Samsung officials said they doubted any announcement on a takeover of Fokker would be made during the airshow.
"I think it will still be too early," said a senior executive who asked not to be identified.

Samsung and the Dutch government have been negotiating the purchase of the aviation pioneer which collapsed on March 15, two months after the aerospace unit of its German parent Daimler Benz AG's decided not to carry Fokker's huge losses.

But officials at Samsung Aerospace said the company expected to sign an engine manufacturing deal with U.S.-based General Electric Co and another with U.S. engine maker Pratt & Whitney during the show.
Major exhibitors at the trade show, which will take place every two years, include U.S.-based McDonnell Douglas, Boeing Corp, British Aerospace Plc and Sukhoi from Russia.

"The Seoul Air Show is designed to lay a solid groundwork for further advancements in the Korean aerospace industry, defence industry and strategic air power," said Major-General Lee Han-ho, director of the show's organising committee.

The South Korean goverment hopes to become a global aerospace player by the year 2005 and has designated aerospace as a strategic industry that domestic firms should enter to strengthen the nation's industrial base.
